catalog_quote: 1.3. Stress Stress placement in monomorphemic words appears to be predictable, and falls on the initial syllable. For example: 'kinya ‘this’, ’jabawu ‘grandfather’, and ’murrkulyi ‘work’. Vowel initial roots also show initial stress: 'uba ‘little’, 'ibal ‘father’, and 'iri ‘woman’. Few monomorphemic words are more than three syllables in length, and those that are generally also have a second stressed syllable on the third syllable, as in 'wana'ngarri ‘stone’, 'balngany'jina ‘thigh’, and 'bulu'mana ‘bullock’. Exceptions to these patterns occur in words which consist of the reduplication of meaningless formatives Such words are normally treated as two phonological words for the purpose of stress assignment, and stress falls in predictable ways onto the separate formatives For example: 'kuny'kuny ‘brains’ and 'buk'buk ‘float’; of course, when the formative is bisyllabic, both methods of stress assignment agree, as in 'mala'mala ‘cheek’. It is beyond the scope of this description to deal with the placement of stress in polymorphemic words Suffice it to remark that some bound morphemes appear to form a phonological word with the root to which they are attached, the whole form being stressed as a single word Other bound morphemes — particularly bisyllabic ones — appear to be independently stressed, and their attachment to a given lexeme has no effect on its stress pattern

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is predictable and falls on the first syllable of the (monomorphemic) word, whether consonant- or vowel-initial; words longer than three syllables generally carry a second stress on the third syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Words of more than three syllables generally also have a second stressed syllable on the third syllable ('wana'ngarri 'stone', 'balngany'jina 'thigh', 'bulu'mana 'bullock').
new_statements.exceptions: Words consisting of reduplicated meaningless formatives are treated as two phonological words, each formative stressed ('kuny'kuny 'brains', 'buk'buk 'float'; 'mala'mala 'cheek' where both analyses agree); some bound morphemes attach to the root and the whole form is stressed as a single word, while other bound morphemes, particularly bisyllabic ones, are independently stressed and do not affect the host's stress pattern. McGregor 2011:100 adds, for Nyulnyulan generally, that some words are not stressed according to the regular pattern.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (monomorphemic words and roots; separate remarks on reduplications and bound morphemes); nothing said about phrase-level stress or citation forms. Source is a short sketch (64 pp.); the statement text was recovered verbatim from public search-inside snippets, not from a full copy, and one clause in the middle of the section (after 'It is beyond the scope of this') is missing.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Warrwa as spoken by its last speakers (McGregor's 1990s fieldwork; the 2026 grammar names Maudie Lennard and Freddy Marker). McGregor 1994 notes two dialects, 'Little Warrwa' (west) and 'Big Warrwa'; Capell 1952/53 calls it 'Warwa' and treats it as a dialect of the same language as Njigina (Nyikina, nyig1240). Glottolog has a single language-level code warr1258 with no dialect codes.

sources.note: Warrwa profile is bibliographic only (names, codes, sources: Capell 1940, 1952/53, n.d; Kerr n.d; Stokes). General remark in the orthography chapter: 'in nearly all words in Kimberley languages the first syllable sounds the loudest (linguists say that it is STRESSED)'; glossary: 'In Australian languages, the first syllable of a word is normally stressed.' Not Warrwa-specific.

sources.note: Discourse-semantics (SFL) comparison of one traditional story per language: theme, reference, conjunction, verbal inflection. Warrwa is coded only for grammatical strategies (pronouns + verbal reference; verbal inflection for Glottolog's most extensive description and RNGE roles; time + concession conjunctions, no addition; tense + verb complexing). Nothing on word stress, accent or tone; nothing usable for the catalog entry (McGregor 1994 fixed rule). McGregor is not cited in the reference list.

sources.citation: McGregor, William B. 2011. The Nyulnyul language of Dampier Land, Western Australia. (Pacific Linguistics 635.) Canberra: ANU. §3.4 Stress, pp. 98-105.
sources.note: Describes Nyulnyul (initial stress plus stress on odd-numbered strong syllables), not Warrwa; Warrwa appears only comparatively: p. 100 'as in many other Nyulnyulan languages, there are words that are not stressed according to the regular pattern'; p. 98 n. 20 Warrwa texts show pitch declination over intonation units (Ross 2006); p. 99 n. 18 Nekes & Worms 2006:67 say accent falls on the first syllable with sometimes a secondary accent on the fourth (Nyulnyul examples).
